s: One of five mountains leaning right over the old town
w: Salzburg keeps five mountains within its limits, and this 508-metre ridge flanks the historic centre from the west, folded into the city's UNESCO World Heritage site. It takes its name from the Benedictine monks of St Peter's Abbey, long settled at its northern foot.
_facts: 508m mountain flanking the western side of Salzburg's historic centre
Part of the city's UNESCO World Heritage Site
Named after the Benedictine monks of St Peter's Abbey at its northern foot

s: One of Europe's largest surviving medieval castles
w: Ordered up by Salzburg's prince-archbishops and hoisted 506 metres above the Salzach, this fortress runs 250 metres long and 150 wide - one of the largest medieval castles left standing anywhere in Europe. It has loomed over the old town for close to a thousand years without ever really giving ground.
_facts: Large medieval fortress built at the behest of Salzburg's prince-archbishops
Sits atop the Festungsberg at 506m altitude
250m long and 150m wide, one of the largest medieval castles in Europe

s: The font where Mozart was baptised
w: Founded in 774 by Saint Vergilius over the remnants of a Roman town, rebuilt after a fire in 1181, then made almost entirely new again in the seventeenth century under Prince-Bishop Wolf Dietrich von Raitenau - this Baroque cathedral still keeps the baptismal font where Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart was christened.
_facts: Baroque cathedral founded 774 by Saint Vergilius over a Roman town
Rebuilt after a fire in 1181, completely rebuilt in Baroque style in the 17th century
Contains the baptismal font in which Mozart was baptized

s: The third-floor rooms where Mozart was born, 1756
w: No. 9 Getreidegasse held the Mozart family from 1747, and it's on the third floor here that Wolfgang Amadeus arrived in January 1756, the seventh child of court musician Leopold Mozart. A museum since 1880, it still keeps his childhood violin and the clavichord on which he composed The Magic Flute.
_facts: House museum at Getreidegasse 9, Salzburg
Mozart family resided here 1747-1773; Wolfgang Amadeus born here 27 January 1756
Museum since 1880, exhibits his childhood violin and the clavichord used for The Magic Flute

s: Salzburg's grandest shopping street, guild signs and all
w: A UNESCO-listed run of tall townhouses in the Altstadt, famous above all for No. 9 - Mozart's birthplace, where he lived until he was seventeen. Wrought-iron guild signs still hang above the shopfronts, a rare survivor of the era when a business was marked by symbol rather than name.
_facts: Historic shopping street in Salzburg's Altstadt, UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1996
Birthplace of Mozart at No. 9, where he lived until age 17
Characterised by high townhouses with wrought-iron guild signs

s: Gothic choir, baroque nave, eighth-century roots
w: One of Salzburg's oldest churches, first raised in the eighth century in the Altstadt. A Gothic choir replaced its Romanesque one between 1408 and 1450, a slender tower followed soon after, and in the eighteenth century Johann Bernhard Fischer von Erlach reworked the interior into full Baroque style.
_facts: One of the oldest churches in Salzburg, first church on the site erected in the 8th century
Gothic choir added 1408-1450 replacing a Romanesque one; Gothic tower added 1468-1498
Interior redesigned in Baroque style by Fischer von Erlach in the 18th century

s: The prince-archbishops' palace, first recorded in 1120
w: For centuries Salzburg's prince-archbishops lived and governed here, using the palace to project their weight across Domplatz and Residenzplatz. It now houses the Residenzgalerie, hung with Rembrandt, Carel Fabritius and Hieronymus Francken II - don't confuse it with the newer Residence across the square.
_facts: Palace first mentioned around 1120, seat of Salzburg's Prince-Archbishops for centuries
Houses the Residenzgalerie art gallery with works by Rembrandt, Carel Fabritius and Hieronymus Francken II
Not to be confused with the nearby Neue Residenz, which houses the Salzburg Museum

s: Vintage warplanes and Formula One cars under one dome
w: Red Bull built this glass-and-steel hangar by the airport to house the Flying Bulls, its private collection of historic aircraft and helicopters, then filled the rest with Formula One racing cars and a rotating art programme. The Michelin-starred restaurant Ikarus sits right inside, so you can dine among the planes.
_facts: Events venue, gallery and museum space beside Salzburg Airport, developed by Red Bull founder Dietrich Mateschitz
Home to the Flying Bulls historic aircraft and helicopter collection, plus Formula One cars
Houses the Michelin-starred restaurant Ikarus

s: Opera, theatre and dance beside the Mirabell Gardens
w: A listed house in the historic Altstadt, staging around 400 performances a season from September to June across opera, theatre and dance. The main hall seats 707, and a staff of 340 people from 35 countries keep the programme running beside the Mirabell Gardens - old-world grandeur, still fully at work.
_facts: Theatre in Salzburg for opera, theatre and dance, next to the Mirabell Gardens
Approximately 400 performances per season, September to June, audience of 707
Listed building, part of the historic Altstadt UNESCO World Heritage Site

s: Salzburg's oldest cemetery, tucked under the fortress crag
w: Set at the foot of the Festungsberg, this is - along with the burial ground at Nonnberg Abbey - the oldest cemetery in Salzburg, and one of its most visited sites. Closed to new burials in 1878, it fell into decay until the monks of St Peter's pushed to reopen it for interments again in 1930.
_facts: St Peter's Cemetery, one of the oldest cemeteries in Salzburg alongside Nonnberg Abbey's burial site
Located at the foot of the Festungsberg beneath Hohensalzburg Castle
Closed in 1878; new burials admitted again from 1930 after monks of St Peter's urged it

s: Where Mozart lived from 17 to 25, Makartplatz 8
w: Leopold Mozart moved the family here in 1773, and it stayed Wolfgang Amadeus's Salzburg home through his late teens and twenties, until 1787. Known as the Tanzmeisterhaus for an earlier dance-master resident, and later the Mozart-Wohnhaus, it's now a protected museum under the Austrian Federal Monuments Office.
_facts: Salzburg home of Leopold Mozart and family from 1773 to 1787, at Makartplatz 8
Home of Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart between ages 17 and 25
Now a museum, protected by the Austrian Federal Monuments Office

s: A prince-archbishop's square, remade for Mozart's statue
w: Wolf Dietrich von Raitenau tore down a row of houses here in the early 1600s to open the square, then called Michaelsplatz; its baroque fountain of St Michael was cleared out in 1841 to make way for the Mozart statue that gives the square its current name. Mozart's widow, Constanze, once lived on its east side.
_facts: Square in Salzburg's Altstadt, formerly Michaelsplatz, created by Prince-Archbishop Wolf Dietrich von Raitenau
Baroque St Michael fountain removed 1841 to make way for the Mozart statue
House number 8 on the east side was home to Constanze Mozart-Nissen, Mozart's widow
